attention-load/cognitive-offload.reason: An independent lab found both halves across three experiments (N = 172 each). Offloading supports 'immediate performance', whereas 'offloading did have detrimental effects on memory without such a goal' (Grinschgl et al. 2021). I found no failed replication of the performance or recall-cost findings; the failed SSRP and Hesselmann replications concern the Google Stroop sub-finding only. There is no meta-analysis, so B. Risko & Gilbert 2016 has no cached abstract; that does not move the grade.

attention-load/job-aid.reason: Urbach et al. 2014 is a natural experiment, neither an RRR nor pre-registered, so tie-break 1 does not strictly apply, and the JSON's tie_break should read 'none'. C holds on the base definition, since the results are mixed (Haynes et al. 2009 positive, Urbach et al. 2014 null). Neither study measures omissions, and Hales & Pronovost and Degani & Wiener have no cached abstract.
attention-load/job-aid.helps_overclaim: player-aid: 'reference aids reduce omissions in procedural work' is stated as settled, but job-aid is C, and no read source measures omissions under a checklist experimentally (Reason 2002 is descriptive). It should be hedged, e.g. 'are used to cut omissions in procedural work, with mixed evidence'.

attention-load/goal-orientation.reason: No counted source tests the claim. The only read evidence, Luiten et al. 1980, concerns advance organisers, which preview material; it does not test stating the question a session must answer. Locke & Latham 2002, Stone 1983, Ausubel 1960 and Rothkopf & Billington 1979 have no cached abstract. This follows the random-stimuli precedent (C → D, 'no counted source tests' the manipulation, accepted at spot-check). Label it D (unread): the goal-setting and adjunct-question literatures may support it once read. The cover's displayed grade falls to D.

attention-load/phone-presence.reason: The Ruiz Pardo & Minda 2022 cached abstract confirms a pre-registered direct replication of Ward et al. Experiment 2 that found no effect. C holds on the base definition ('a failed replication') even if its n is below twice the original's, so tie-break 1 is not needed.

attention-load/stop-mid-task.reason: The Ghibellini & Meier 2025 cached abstract supports only a general tendency to resume. Ease of resumption, stopping mid-sentence and gaps of days are untested.

attention-load/resumption-cues.reason: A meta-analysis of 33 laboratory experiments found interruption interventions 'significantly increased primary task accuracy (standardized mean difference (SMD) = 1.03, P = 0.001) and reduced resumption lag (SMD = -0.51, P < 0.001)', with effects varying 'by the type of intervention' (abstract via PubMed). This covers the claim's errors half too. The abstract pools cues with other interventions and gives no cue-only estimate, so it cannot lift the grade. I found no failed replication.

attention-load/task-switching.reason: This is the lower edge of B. The Rogers & Monsell 1995 cached abstract gives a switch cost that preparation reduced but did not remove. I found no failed replication of switch costs themselves. The Wiradhany & Nieuwenstein 2017 null concerns an individual-difference claim about media multitaskers, not switch cost. Kiesel et al. 2010's abstract states the review's scope only.
